structures.title: Basic statement word order
structures.explanation: Spanish default order is SVO, just like English. Because verb endings show the person, the subject pronoun is usually dropped unless needed for emphasis or clarity. Word order is flexible for emphasis.
structures.ex2_ref: I drink coffee in the morning.

structures.title: Forming a yes/no question
structures.explanation: You can turn a statement into a question just by adding question marks and a rising intonation; word order need not change. Spanish also uses an inverted opening mark ¿. Optionally the subject moves after the verb.

structures.title: Negation and double negatives
structures.explanation: Put no directly before the verb to negate it. When a negative word like nada, nadie or nunca follows the verb, no must still appear before it, creating a required double negative.

structures.title: Expressing the near future
structures.explanation: Conjugate ir (voy/vas/va/vamos/vais/van), add a, then the infinitive to say what is going to happen. It is the most common way to talk about future plans in speech, like English 'going to'.
structures.ex2_ref: We are going to travel in summer.

structures.title: Action happening right now
structures.explanation: Combine estar with the gerund (-ando for -ar verbs, -iendo for -er/-ir) to stress an action in progress at this moment. It is used less than the English '-ing' and never for future plans.
structures.ex2_target: Los niños están jugando en el jardín.
structures.ex2_ref: The children are playing in the garden.

structures.title: Saying what you like
structures.explanation: Gustar means 'to be pleasing', so the liked thing is the grammatical subject. Use gusta before a singular noun or an infinitive and gustan before a plural noun; the person is an indirect object pronoun.
structures.ex2_target: A ella le gustan los perros.

structures.title: Saying there is / there are
structures.explanation: Hay is an invariable form of haber meaning 'there is' or 'there are'; it never changes for singular or plural. Use it to state existence or, in a question, to ask whether something exists.

structures.title: First conditional (real situations)
structures.explanation: For a likely condition, use si + present tense in the 'if' clause and the present or future in the result clause. Note there is no accent on si ('if'), unlike sí ('yes').
structures.ex1_target: Si tengo tiempo, voy al gimnasio.
structures.ex1_ref: If I have time, I go to the gym.
structures.ex2_ref: If it rains, we won't go out.

structures.title: Making comparisons
structures.explanation: Place más ('more') or menos ('less') before the adjective and que ('than') after it to compare two things. Use tan ... como for 'as ... as'. A few adjectives have irregular comparatives like mejor and peor.
structures.ex1_target: Ella es más alta que yo.
structures.ex1_ref: She is taller than I am.
structures.ex2_target: Este coche es menos caro que el otro.
structures.ex2_ref: This car is less expensive than the other one.

structures.title: Expressing obligation
structures.explanation: Conjugate tener and add que plus an infinitive to say what someone has to do. For impersonal obligation ('one must') use hay que + infinitive instead.

structures.title: Relative clause with que
structures.explanation: Que links a describing clause to a noun and covers English 'that', 'which' and 'who'. Unlike English, que can never be omitted, and it works for both people and things.
structures.ex1_target: El hombre que vive aquí es médico.
structures.ex1_ref: The man who lives here is a doctor.
structures.ex2_target: La casa que compramos es antigua.
structures.ex2_ref: The house that we bought is old.

structures.title: Wanting someone else to do something
structures.explanation: When you want another person to do something, use querer + que + a verb in the present subjunctive. The two clauses have different subjects; a same-subject wish uses a plain infinitive (quiero ir).
structures.ex2_ref: We want you to be happy.

structures.title: Passive voice with ser
structures.explanation: Form the true passive with ser plus a past participle that agrees in gender and number with the subject; the doer is introduced by por. It is more formal than the everyday se-passive.
structures.ex1_target: La carta fue escrita por María.
structures.ex1_ref: The letter was written by María.

structures.title: Reported (indirect) speech
structures.explanation: Introduce reported statements with decir que. When the reporting verb is in the past, the verb in the reported clause typically shifts to a past tense, mirroring English backshift.
structures.ex1_ref: He said that he was tired.
structures.ex2_ref: He says he will arrive late.

structures.title: Superlative (the most ... of)
structures.explanation: Use the definite article plus más (or menos) plus the adjective, followed by de for the group compared. The article agrees with the noun, and 'in/of' is always de, never en.
structures.ex1_target: Es el más alto de la clase.
structures.ex1_ref: He is the tallest in the class.
structures.ex2_target: Es la ciudad más grande del país.
structures.ex2_ref: It is the biggest city in the country.

structures.title: Concession (although / even though)
structures.explanation: Aunque introduces a contrast. Use the indicative for a known fact ('although it is raining, and it really is') and the subjunctive for a hypothetical or downplayed possibility ('even if it should rain').
structures.ex1_ref: Although it's raining, I'm going out.
structures.ex2_ref: Even if it's difficult, I'll try it.
